name: Coinrail
notes: In June 2018 the Korean exchange Coinrail reported a 'cyber intrusion' that took the roughly 30% of reserves it held outside cold storage: ERC-20 tokens such as NPXS, ATX and DENT plus ETH, about $37-40M. The attacker moved the funds directly and no user signed anything. The exact intrusion method was never published.

name: PlayDapp
malicious_action: attacker added itself as minter/owner on the PLA token contract and minted 1.79B PLA
notes: PlayDapp's post-mortem says the hacker obtained the PLA contract's private key, moved ownership and mint rights to their own account, and minted 200M then 1.59B PLA. The headline $290M is notional; the attacker could actually cash out about $32M.

name: US Permissionless Dollar
notes: USPD deployed its proxy and initialized it in separate transactions. On Sep 16, 2025 the attacker front-ran the initialization through Multicall3 and slipped in a hidden 'CPIMP' middle proxy that forwarded calls to the audited code; on Dec 4, 2025 he upgraded it, minted about 98M USPD and drained about 232 stETH (about $1M). No key was stolen and no signer was tricked; the flaw was in the deployment sequence.

name: Fake GIWA Bridge
malicious_action: ETH deposited into a scammer-run fake GIWA OptimismPortal (0xba9938c0…5ab2)
notes: Scammers launched a fake OP-Stack chain on GIWA's reserved chain ID 9134, with an L1 portal contract that emitted genuine-looking TransactionDeposited events. After DYORSWAP listed it as GIWA mainnet, 1,335 addresses deposited about 767 ETH, which the operators withdrew on 27 Sep 2026. The deposits did exactly what they encoded; users were wrong about who ran the chain.

name: Terraport
notes: On Apr 10, 2023 Terraport, a Terra Classic DEX, said 'a breach was detected in the Terraport Liquidity wallet', and about $4M of LUNC, USTC and TERRA liquidity was pulled out in two transactions. SlowMist lists it as a contract vulnerability, but I found no post-mortem that settles whether it was a contract bug, a key compromise or an insider.

name: Solrise Finance
notes: The record's name looks mislabelled: the 26 July 2024, $6.7M Casper-chain incident is the Casper Network breach. Attackers used a node-software bug that let a contract installer bypass URef access-rights checks, escalating privileges to transfer tokens out of 13 wallets; validators halted and patched the network, with no keys compromised.

name: FixedFloat
notes: About $26.1M in BTC and ETH was moved out of FixedFloat's addresses in Feb 2024. FixedFloat blamed a third party exploiting gaps in its infrastructure, which is consistent with hot-wallet key theft; there was no public post-mortem and no user signing.

name: Tapioca DAO
notes: A DPRK 'contagious interview' (fake LinkedIn recruiter, malicious .env file) put malware on the lead contract engineer's machine and stole his hot-wallet key, which alone held admin over TAP's vesting contract and USDO. The attacker seized the vesting contract and added a USDO minter, draining ~$4.65M.

name: JayPegs Automart
malicious_action: MISO createMarket whose auction-wallet parameter was replaced with attacker address 0x3dDD8b6D092df917473680d6C41F80F708C45395 by injected frontend code
notes: This was the SushiSwap MISO supply-chain attack: a contractor injected code into the MISO frontend that replaced the auction wallet with his own address. The auction creator (0xF33b…aE5c) signed createMarket on Sep 10, 2021 with the attacker address in the encoded data, and that creator's finalize() on Sep 16 paid 864.8 ETH to the attacker, who returned it after being identified. The createMarket hash was found on Etherscan by tracing the attacker address that rekt cites.

name: Coinbene
notes: Coinbene went into 'maintenance' while roughly $45M of ERC-20 tokens (mostly Maximine Coin and Coinbene Coin) left its wallets and were dumped on other exchanges. The exchange said it was targeted by hackers but called funds secure and never explained how; this is inferred to be an exchange hot-wallet compromise, with no deceived signer.

name: TermFinance Vaults
malicious_action: Aragon TokenVoting proposal disguised as a routine 'Veto strategy vault parameter change' with 17 actions: set the Zodiac Delay cooldown and expiration to zero, enable the attacker as executor, recall funds from the real strategies, add an attacker 'strategy' with a uint256-max debt limit, and push the vault's balance into it
notes: Almost no depositors had wrapped their vault shares into the governance token, so a ~0.5 ETH deposit gave the attacker ~91% of the ETH Meta Vault's voting supply (and all of it in several USDC vaults). Executed Aug 23, 2026 (txs 0xd354a15b...4129 and 0x9f273f9a...e8a0), draining ~2,843 WETH and 1.68M USDC (~$8.5M).

name: CoinsPaid
notes: CoinsPaid attributed the July 22, 2023 theft of $37.3M of company (not customer) funds to Lazarus. DeFiLlama labels the entry vector a recruiter-impersonation scam. The attackers broke into company systems and moved funds themselves; no external signer review step was reported.

name: Vowcurrency
notes: While the team tested the vUSD contract's USD-rate setter on mainnet, the rate was briefly raised. Within that 15-30 second window a bot bought ~20M VOW and sent it to the contract, minting nearly v$2B that it sold into Uniswap (~$1.2M): a team misconfiguration exploited by a third party, not signing deception.

name: Hector Network
notes: In January 2024 about $2.7M in USDC left Hector Network's redemption contract, which was meant to pay holders after the DAO's rage-quit, after an address not on the recipient list was marked eligible in the contract. The team never explained it, so a setup error, misuse of a privileged key and an insider cannot be told apart.

name: Aperture LM
notes: An arbitrary-call flaw in a helper module of Aperture's closed-source V3/V4 contracts let the attacker make the contract call transferFrom on users' existing ERC-20 and Uniswap LP-NFT approvals, draining ~$3.67M across chains. No new victim signatures were involved.

name: TempleDAO
notes: TempleDAO's staking contract function migrateStake did not validate the oldStaking address. The attacker passed a fake contract to credit themselves an arbitrary balance and withdrew ~$2.3M.

name: Ankr
notes: Ankr's deployer private key was compromised and used to mint ~60 trillion aBNBc, which were dumped for ~$5M of BNB. Ankr's after-action report says a former team member combined social engineering with a malicious code package slipped into a legitimate update to steal the key: insider key theft, not deception of signers.

name: FEG Token
notes: FEG's swapToSwap() trusted a user-supplied 'path' address and let it spend the contract's assets. The attacker combined flash loans with depositInternal()/swapToSwap() to drain ~$1.9M on BSC and Ethereum, the second such attack in two days.

name: Shido
notes: With a compromised owner key, the attacker transferred ownership of the StakingV4Proxy, upgraded it with a hidden withdrawToken() function, and withdrew ~4.35B SHIDO (~$3.3M once sold).

name: Gym Network
notes: A newly added 'Claim and Pool' feature in GymSinglePool did not verify the caller, so the attacker could credit himself deposits without paying and then withdraw them, about $2.1M (about 7.5K BNB).

name: GeniusAI
notes: GNUS.ai said a hacker minted fake GNUS on Fantom, bridged them through Axelar to Ethereum and Polygon, and sold them into pools (~$1.27M). SlowMist and Halborn call it a contract vulnerability, but DeFiLlama labels it a social account takeover and no root-cause post-mortem was found.

name: Stake.com
malicious_action: unauthorized hot-wallet transactions after a breach of Stake's transaction-authorization service
notes: The FBI attributed the theft of about $41M from Stake's ETH, BSC and Polygon hot wallets to Lazarus. The co-founder says the attacker breached the service Stake uses to authorize transactions rather than the keys themselves; either way it was an automated signing path with no human reviewer.

name: Tornado Cash
notes: The attacker's proposal claimed to match an earlier approved one but hid selfdestruct and redeploy logic. Once it passed, they swapped in code that granted them 1.2M votes, took over governance, and withdrew about 483k TORN (~$2.2M).

name: Wasabi Perps
malicious_action: compromised deployer granted ADMIN_ROLE to a malicious contract and UUPS-upgraded vault and pool contracts
notes: Wasabi's deployer EOA held the sole ADMIN_ROLE with no multisig or timelock. The attacker who obtained that key gave admin rights to a prepared contract and upgraded PerpManager and LongPool on four chains, draining about $5M. How the key was stolen is undisclosed.

name: LuBian
notes: LuBian mining-pool wallets were generated with a weak, predictable PRNG (MT19937-based), so their keys could be recomputed; on 2020-12-28 the coins (~127k-137k BTC) were swept in about two hours, which Milk Sad calls a likely theft. No victim signing step; whoever held the recomputed keys signed directly.

name: Kannagi
notes: Kannagi Finance, a zkSync Era yield aggregator, rug-pulled ~$2.1M using a MainChef function that could withdraw on behalf of any user. It bridged the proceeds to Ethereum (0x95ec03b821f164ce55cbb26f23f591a9bd40d6c1) and deleted its website and social accounts.

name: DAO Maker Vesting
notes: DAO Maker's vesting/distribution contracts left init() unprotected. The attacker re-initialised them, made themselves owner and called emergencyExit to pull DERC, CPD, CAPS and SHO tokens (~$4M); this was a pure contract bug, unlike DAO Maker's separate August 2021 admin-key incident.

name: Compounder Finance
notes: Compounder's developers used their own 24-hour timelock to swap audited strategy contracts for 'evil' strategies without withdrawal restrictions, pulled about $12M of user funds, and deleted the project's channels.

name: GDAC
notes: Hackers moved ~$13M out of GDAC's hot wallet, signing with access they had obtained to it.

name: M2 Exchange
notes: About $13.7M was stolen from several of M2's on-chain hot wallets (ETH, SOL, BTC); a hot-wallet compromise with no deceived signer.

name: Solareum
notes: In late March 2024, users of the Solareum Telegram trading bot, which held their private keys, had their wallets drained (~$1M+). The cause was never confirmed; leaked bot tokens exposing keys were suspected, and the team denied theft and shut down. No user signed anything.

name: Fetch.ai
malicious_action: compromised trusted backend signing key authorized conversionIn releasing 8.72M FET
notes: A leaked backend authorization key that the TokenConversionManagerV3 contract trusted (SingularityNET's Ethereum-Cardano bridge infrastructure) was used to withdraw about 8.72M FET (about $1.55M). The same actor used a stolen NuNet minter key to mint 408.5M NTX 29 minutes later.

name: Nemo Yield Trading
notes: Nemo's yield-trading market pool on Sui was drained of about $2.4M on Sept 7-8, 2025 through on-chain price manipulation (Web3 Is Going Great describes it as oracle manipulation). No key compromise or victim signature was reported. I could not read the detailed root-cause post-mortem.

name: GateHub
notes: An attacker got access to GateHub backend/API permissions and drained ~23.2M XRP from user XRP Ledger wallets by signing transactions directly; users signed nothing.

name: Impermax
notes: A hacker obtained private keys to several team-controlled wallets and took ~9M IMX plus protocol-owned liquidity; Impermax migrated to a new token (IBEX).

name: Remilia
notes: The treasury multisig's keys were all kept in one password manager, which the founder says was compromised (suspected malware); the attacker drained ~490 ETH plus Milady/Remilio NFTs. Some observers suspected an inside job.

name: Cryptsy
malicious_action: BTC and LTC drained from exchange wallets via a trojaned Lucky7Coin wallet
notes: Cryptsy's CEO said in January 2016 that the new Lucky7Coin developer had planted an IRC backdoor in the coin's wallet software. He said the trojan was used on July 29, 2014 to take about 13,000 BTC and 300,000 LTC from wallets on the same machine. This account came 18 months later as the exchange collapsed, so it is self-reported.

name: Curve Finance MEV Bot
notes: An MEV bot contract had a public function (selector 0xf6ebebbb) with no access control that could trigger swaps in Curve pools. The attacker used it to make the bot trade at prices he had pumped and took about $2M. Nobody signed anything.

name: CoinsPaid
notes: Second CoinsPaid breach (Jan 2024, ~$7.5M in USDT/ETH/USDC/BNB/CPD). Cyvers blamed inadequate wallet access control and suspected Lazarus; attacker-signed withdrawals with no deceived signer.

name: Dragoma
notes: The only source available was DeFiLlama's dataset, which labels this a Rugpull/Admin Drain of ~$3.5M on Polygon. No independent post-mortem could be found or read, so the classification is inferred.

name: Munchables
notes: A rogue developer the team had hired (ZachXBT linked four 'devs' to one person, suspected DPRK) kept control of the upgradeable proxy. Before switching to a legitimate-looking implementation he wrote himself a 1,000,000 ETH deposit balance through storage slots, then withdrew about $62.5M. He later handed back the keys and all funds were recovered.

name: Bitrue
notes: A hacker exploited a flaw in Bitrue's risk-control second-review process to reach about 90 users' funds, then used that access to get into the exchange hot wallet and move 9.3M XRP and 2.5M ADA to other exchanges. An exchange system and hot-wallet breach, with no deceived user or signer.

name: Furucombo
notes: Furucombo's proxy delegatecalled a whitelisted handler, the Aave V2 proxy, whose initialize let the attacker set the implementation slot in Furucombo's own storage. His code then pulled about $14M in tokens from users who had approved the Furucombo proxy. The losses came from those standing approvals, which rekt says were largely 'infinite' (unlimited).

name: Concentric
notes: Concentric said a targeted social-engineering attack on the team member holding the deployer wallet compromised that wallet. The attacker used it to upgrade the vaults, mint LP tokens and drain ~$1.7M; there is no report of a disguised transaction being signed.

name: 3Commas
notes: An attacker obtained users' exchange API keys from 3Commas's database and used them to trade on linked exchange accounts without authorization (about $20M). API-key theft; no user signed anything.

name: COLDCARD
notes: A 2021 firmware build error made some Coldcards generate seeds from a weak software RNG (as low as ~40 bits). Attackers enumerated the keyspace and swept ~1,800 BTC from thousands of addresses (Jul 30-Aug 3, 2026) without touching any device.

name: DuelBits
notes: The crypto casino Duelbits lost about $4.6M from its hot wallets in Feb 2024. SlowMist records it as a hot-wallet private-key leak, and the attacker signed directly.

name: Coinsbuy
notes: On Aug 9, 2026 eleven Coinsbuy hot wallets on TRON and Ethereum were drained of about $8M, starting with a 5 USDT test transfer. Coinsbuy has not disclosed how. GoPlus said the pattern fits a hot-wallet key or admin-privilege compromise, but Coinsbuy refilled the same addresses within a day, and rekt notes nothing public tells apart key theft, abuse of an API or signing system, or an insider.

name: KICKICO
notes: Hackers got the private key of the KickCoin token contract owner and used owner powers to move ~$7.7M of KICK out of holders' balances. No victim signed anything.

name: pump.fun
notes: A former employee used privileged access he still had, plus flash loans, to drain ~$1.9M from pump.fun bonding curves.

name: Mintpal
notes: An attacker used SQL injection against MintPal's systems to authorise a withdrawal of the exchange's VeriCoin hot wallet: 8M VRC (~$1.8M), much of which had wrongly been left out of cold storage. VeriCoin hard-forked to recover; this was an exchange hot-wallet system breach with no deceived signer.

name: SUNRAY·FINANCE
notes: With a leaked private key, the attacker upgraded Sunray's contract, minted a huge SUN supply, and sold SUN/ARC into DEX pools (~$2.86M).

name: Moby
malicious_action: compromised proxy-admin key used to transfer ownership, upgrade contracts and call emergencyWithdrawERC20
notes: On Jan 8, 2025 an attacker holding the private key behind Moby's proxy contracts transferred ownership, upgraded the contracts and withdrew about $2.5M with emergencyWithdrawERC20. A whitehat recovered part of it because of a flaw in the attacker's upgrade.

name: KITE Foundation
notes: Monitoring flagged abnormal KITE transfers from compromised wallets on Ethereum; the foundation froze transfers and the bridge, then migrated to a new contract that excluded attacker addresses, and says no tokens were lost. How the wallets were compromised is undisclosed, so the vector cannot be determined.

name: MEV-Boost Relay
notes: A malicious proposer exploited a vulnerability in the mev-boost-relay software: by signing an invalid block header it got the relay to reveal the block body, then unbundled and sandwiched MEV bots' transactions for about $20-25M. This was a relay software bug, not leaked keys, and no victim signed anything.

name: Ooki
notes: This is the November 2021 bZx incident (bZx later became Ooki). A developer opened a macro-laden Word attachment from a phishing email, malware stole his mnemonic, and the attacker used the keys controlling the Polygon and BSC deployments to upgrade contracts, drain the protocol, and take funds from users who had granted unlimited approvals.

name: Levyathan
notes: Developers left the private key of a wallet with LEV minting rights in a public GitHub repo. About four months later an attacker used it to mint and dump LEV (July 2021), and a buggy emergencyWithdraw made user losses worse.

name: Shibarium
malicious_action: fraudulent bridge checkpoint signed with 10 of 12 compromised validator keys
notes: The attacker controlled 10 of Shibarium's 12 validator signing keys, took a 4.6M BONE flash loan for stake weight, and signed a fraudulent checkpoint that released about $2.4M from the Ethereum bridge. How the validator keys were compromised has not been disclosed.

name: OKX DEX
notes: The Proxy Admin Owner's private key leaked; the attacker upgraded a deprecated DEX proxy to call claimTokens on TokenApprove and pulled tokens through users' old approvals (~$2.7M). Users signed nothing at attack time.

name: Lykke
malicious_action: hot wallets drained (about 158 BTC, 2,161 ETH and other assets)
notes: Lykke's hot wallets on several chains were drained of about $22M on June 4, 2024 and the exchange later went into liquidation. No root cause was published; the DPRK attribution is disputed.

name: BTC.com
notes: BIT Mining reported a Dec 3, 2022 cyberattack on its BTC.com pool in which about $700k of customer assets and $2.3M of company assets were stolen. Infrastructure compromise; no victim signing.

name: Poloniex
notes: An attacker holding the hot-wallet private keys drained ~$126M from Poloniex hot wallets on Ethereum, TRON and Bitcoin; the theft is attributed to Lazarus. No victim signing step was involved.

name: StakeHound / Fireblocks
notes: Not an attack and not a theft: per StakeHound, custodian errors by Fireblocks lost 2 of the 3-of-4 threshold key shares (not generated in production and not properly backed up), leaving 38,178 staked ETH inaccessible. No vector fits, so UNKNOWN; DeFiLlama's 'Key Brute Forced' label is not supported by any source.

name: EigenLayer
malicious_action: Safe execTransaction (operation=1 delegatecall to MultiSendCallOnly 0x40A2aCCbd92BCA938b02010E17A5b8929b49130D) batching 12 EIGEN transfer() calls, one of which sent 1,673,644.67 EIGEN to attacker address 0xa7a1c66168cC0b5fC78721157F513c89697Df10D, substituted through a compromised email thread
notes: An email thread about one investor's token transfer into custody was compromised, so signers of distribution Safe 0x87787389BB2Eb2EC8Fe4aA6a2e33D671d925A60f paid the attacker's address inside an otherwise normal batch on Oct 4, 2024. The bytes did exactly what they said; the recipient sold the EIGEN through DEXes that day, and Etherscan flags it as under investigation by EigenLayer. Hash found from on-chain logs and confirmed on Etherscan.

name: Mt. Gox
malicious_action: unauthorized hot-wallet withdrawals using private keys stolen from the wallet server
notes: According to the DOJ, hackers broke into the Mt. Gox server holding its wallets and private keys in September 2011 and drained about 647,000 BTC between then and 2014. The exchange collapsed in February 2014.

name: Cashaa
notes: Malware on a Cashaa system alerted the hacker when an employee logged into the exchange's Blockchain.com wallet on July 10, 2020; two transfers then moved 336 BTC to the hacker. Remote-access/key compromise; no deceived signer.

name: NFPrompt
notes: Hackers compromised several wallets, including the NFP contract administrators' wallets, and made unauthorized withdrawals from the treasury and user accounts. The FBI investigated, and an FBI complaint reported by Forbes reportedly tied the theft to North Korean malware (CryptoMimic).

name: UPCX
notes: Someone gained control of a UPCX management address (0x4C...3583E), used it to perform a malicious upgrade of the ProxyAdmin contract, then called withdrawByAdmin to move 18.4M UPC (~$70M) from three management accounts. Halborn and BlockThreat attribute this to a stolen private key (UPCX never published a root cause), and UPCX later said the 18,473,290 UPC remained under project control.

name: Beanstalk
malicious_action: Malicious proposal (BIP-18) passed with flash-loaned voting power and executed immediately via emergencyCommit, sending protocol assets to the attacker
notes: A flash-loan governance attack. Beanstalk had no delay between a vote and its execution, so the attacker borrowed enough to win the vote and, in one transaction, passed and executed a proposal that drained ~$182M of protocol assets (~$80M net to the attacker).

name: DogWifTools
notes: With a stolen GitHub token, the attacker published trojanized DogWifTools releases (v1.6.3-1.6.6) that contained a RAT. The RAT harvested users' private keys and exchange logins, which were then used to drain about $10M.

name: Crypto DAO
notes: The Pro token's vault contract (0xc44f2a...) exposed an exec() function with no access control. The attacker called it repeatedly in one transaction to swap the contract's Pro into USDT, pumping the pair before selling; GoPlus and SlowMist put the real profit near $52K (167,200 Pro), and the $8.2M figure is balances held by linked addresses.

name: Uniswap (Phishing Attack)
malicious_action: setApprovalForAll on Uniswap V3 Positions NFT (NonfungiblePositionManager) to attacker 0x3cafc86a…97a2 (Fake_Phishing5877)
notes: A fake 'UniswapLP' token airdropped to 73,399 Uniswap V3 LPs pointed to a phishing 'claim' site. The large victim 0xecc6…4eba signed setApprovalForAll for their position NFTs (two identical txs at 20:09 UTC on 11 Jul 2022). The operator then moved the NFTs to 0x09b5…7afa, which removed the liquidity (~$8M) and laundered it through Tornado Cash. Hashes were traced on-chain from the attacker address The Block published and confirmed on Etherscan.

name: 8ightDAO
notes: 8ight Finance, an OHM fork on Harmony, lost its whole treasury (~$1.75M) after treasury private keys leaked. Its developers had shared them over Facebook chat and Google Drive. The attacker signed directly.

name: VeChain
malicious_action: about 1.1B VET moved out of the VeChain Foundation buyback account
notes: VeChain said a finance-team member set up the buyback address without following its standard procedure (no multisig), and blamed 'misconduct' by that team member; about 1.1B VET (about $6.5M) was taken. It never said whether an outsider or an insider used the key.

name: Livecoin
notes: Livecoin said a 'carefully planned attack' took control of all its servers, backend and nodes around Dec 24, 2020 (prices on the exchange were manipulated), and it later shut down. Infrastructure takeover (some suspected an exit scam); no user signing.

name: Seedify
malicious_action: stolen developer key used to take ownership of the SFUND OFT bridge contract and mint unbacked SFUND
notes: Seedify says DPRK-linked hackers got one of its developers' private keys and used it to take ownership of the SFUND OFT bridge contract. They minted unbacked SFUND on Avalanche and drained pools on several chains.

name: Garden
notes: Garden's forensic report says a solver operator's private key leaked from a compromised device (SSH logs show access from multiple IPs), letting the attacker drain about $11.4M of solver inventory on Oct 30, 2025. User funds were not affected and nobody was tricked into signing.

name: CoinTiger (PTT)
notes: During routine verification, CoinTiger found that the cold wallet holding Proton (PTT) had been hacked and 401,981,748 PTT stolen (Aug 2019). Exchange wallet key compromise; no user signing.

name: MM Finance Cronos
malicious_action: approve to an attacker router (0xbd872533db178ff7657bf0057f25abc4ff6f904c) injected into the frontend, then swap/addLiquidity/removeLiquidity calls to it that forwarded the tokens to the attacker
notes: Through a DNS vulnerability the attacker changed the router address in MM.Finance's hosted files (May 4, 2022). Users approved the fake router and called it with normal-looking router calldata (recipient = themselves), but it sent their tokens and LP proceeds to 0xb306…9a6b. The example pair is one victim's (0xa6e1…7bda) USDC approve to the fake router and a swapExactTokensForETH that sent the USDC to the attacker. I traced both on-chain via Cronos RPC from the attacker address in the post-mortem, so the hashes themselves are not quoted in a source.

name: EtherCrash
notes: EtherCrash said its 'cold' wallet was compromised and 6,378 ETH (~$2.5M) left in two large withdrawals, then swapped to DAI on Uniswap.

name: Gatecoin
notes: In May 2016 attackers breached the systems of Hong Kong exchange Gatecoin and drained its hot wallets, about 185,000 ETH and 250 BTC (about $2M). They had also changed the system so that ETH deposits skipped the multisig cold storage and went straight to the hot wallet.

name: BTER
malicious_action: 7,170 BTC taken from the exchange's cold wallet system
notes: In February 2015 BTER lost 7,170 BTC (about $1.75M) from its cold wallet system after what it called an attack on a managed server. It is unclear how the keys were obtained, and some accounts allege employees were involved.

name: Grand Base
notes: Grand Base's deployer private key was leaked or stolen. The attacker used its minting rights to create about 32.5M GB and drained about $1.7M from the Base liquidity pools.

name: MyAlgo
notes: About 25 high-value MyAlgo accounts that used mnemonic wallets with keys stored in the browser were drained (about $9.2M, Feb 19-21, 2023) by an attacker who had obtained their keys. MyAlgo had not confirmed a root cause in these reports (DeFiLlama records a CDN compromise); victims did not sign the theft transactions.

name: Phantom Galaxies
malicious_action: 0.1 ETH 'mint fee' sent as a plain ETH transfer to scammer EOA 0x5b54e19f…4ae1 from a fake mint site
notes: A malware bot beat a Phantom Galaxies Discord admin's 2FA, and the attacker announced a fake NFT mint. About 1,571 payments of 0.1 ETH, 265 ETH in all, went as plain transfers with empty calldata to the scammer's address. Victims signed exactly what their wallets showed; they were wrong about who they were paying.

name: Badger DAO
malicious_action: unlimited increaseAllowance (approve for the largest vault) to attacker EOA 0x1fcdb04d0c5364fbd92c73ca8af9baa72c269107
notes: An unauthorized Cloudflare Workers API key let the attacker inject a script into Badger's app that added unlimited ERC-20 approvals to users' deposit and claim flows: approve for the largest vault, increaseAllowance for the others, because MetaMask did not show increaseAllowance as an approval. About 500 wallets approved the attacker EOA, which drained about $120M with transferFrom on Dec 2, 2021. 0x5e4c… is the Celsius-labelled victim's increaseAllowance(attacker, maxUint) on byvWBTC (Dec 1, linked by rekt); 0x3cad… is a bSLP increaseAllowance from Nov 20 (cited by Microsoft). Both were verified on Etherscan.

name: Resolv USR
notes: The attacker compromised Resolv's AWS KMS environment, which held the single private key that authorizes USR mints (reportedly entered through a contractor's compromised GitHub credential). They signed completeSwap calls minting about 80M unbacked USR against $100-200k of collateral and extracted about $23-25M.

name: CoinDash
malicious_action: ETH sent to the attacker address that replaced the official ICO address on the hacked website
notes: Minutes into the July 17, 2017 ICO, an attacker changed CoinDash's website to show his own ETH address (0x6a16…ae48), and contributors sent about 43,400 ETH there. These were plain ETH transfers that did exactly what they said: victims were deceived about the recipient. The example contributor transfers (92.3 ETH and 0.6 ETH) were read on Etherscan for the address BleepingComputer names as the hacker's; Etherscan flags it as compromised, and it later sent 10,000 and 20,000 ETH back to 0x5AC2…7F08.

name: XBridge
notes: Anyone could call XBridge's listToken for a small fee and be recorded as that token's owner, and withdrawTokens then let the owner pull the bridge's entire balance of it. The attacker listed STC and other tokens this way and withdrew them, about $1.44M across Ethereum and BSC.

name: DMM Bitcoin
malicious_action: 2-of-3 P2SH-P2WSH multisig spend of 9 UTXOs (8x500 + 503 BTC) from 3P8MfdM4pULv7ozdQvfwAqNF29zAjmnUYD, paying 4,502.9 BTC in a single output to 1B6rJRfjTXwEy36SCs5zofGMmdv2kdZw7P, a vanity lookalike of DMM's usual destination 1B6rJ6ZKfZmkqMyBGe5KR27oWkEbQdNM7P (same first 5 and last 2 characters)
notes: Per the FBI and Japan's NPA, TraderTraitor (DPRK) gave an employee of Ginco, DMM's wallet-software vendor, a fake pre-employment test, hijacked his session, and manipulated a legitimate DMM transaction request. The signed transaction faithfully paid a lookalike address, which points to DECEIVED_INTENT; it would be SIGNING_DECEPTION_MULTISIG if the signing interface itself showed DMM's real address, which is not publicly confirmed. The txid is in rekt.news and was verified on blockstream.info: block 845859, 0.1 BTC fee.

name: Chain Fusion
notes: The private key of Fusion's swap wallet was stolen and 10M native FSN plus 3.5M ERC-20 FSN were moved out; Fusion said it suspected someone with access to the keys, so likely an insider.

name: BtcTurk
malicious_action: withdrawals from 10 hot wallets
notes: BtcTurk said a cyber attack on June 22, 2024 drained part of the balances in 10 hot wallets (about $55M) while cold wallets were unaffected; Halborn attributes it to likely compromised private keys. No root cause was published.

name: Duelbits
malicious_action: hot wallets on Ethereum, BNB Chain, Tron and Bitcoin drained
notes: About $7M left Duelbits' hot wallets within minutes on Sept 24, 2026; Scam Sniffer assessed it as a suspected private-key compromise. Duelbits has not published a root cause.

name: Cryptopia
notes: A hot-wallet private key was compromised and about NZ$24M was taken; the perpetrator was never identified (co-founders suspected someone with internal knowledge). No victim signing step.

name: Fetch.ai
malicious_action: hackers in Fetch.ai's Binance accounts traded and transferred about $2.6M of assets
notes: On June 6-7, 2021 unknown parties got into Fetch.ai's accounts on Binance and moved or traded USDT, BNB, BTC and FET worth about $2.6M; a London court ordered Binance to help identify them. This was an exchange account takeover, not an on-chain signature.

name: BonkDAO
malicious_action: Realms/SPL Governance proposal BIP #76 'Sowellian BonkDAO' carrying a transferChecked of 4,426,104,450,305 BONK from the DAO treasury to attacker wallet 9bxWkNf3BtJ6iehq9KbX9uCWMjem4TFiPZ19T2sYJHvQ
notes: An attacker bought just over 1% of BONK supply (~$4.4M) to clear a 1% quorum. With a zero-second instruction hold-up time, the treasury transfer executed as soon as the vote closed (Solana tx 5tPU1srcRcnmibB7KJi2WQ7cK4zuq5iKTMrSCLjq7hvGjuK4KUTmaHfwicixkJa5jZJmp3y98T7r2qecKV5mWw8P, verified via RPC).

name: Heco Bridge
malicious_action: HECO bridge drained through a compromised operator account
notes: About $86.6M was drained through the HECO bridge's compromised operator account on Nov 22, 2023, alongside the HTX hot-wallet theft. An FBI complaint says APT38 tricked an HTX employee into running a malicious GitHub app and then backdoored an HTX server.

name: TesseraDAO
notes: On June 1, 2026, on BNB Chain, a single admin key with total authority (no multisig, no timelock, audit never completed) was used to reassign the trader and withdrawer roles, call transferOwnership, mint 99M TSR and dump it for about $2.49M. Reports and QuillAudits call it a stolen or compromised admin key, but the anonymous team never commented and rekt suggests the key holder may have done it, so an insider exit cannot be ruled out.

name: AlphaPo
notes: Private keys of AlphaPo's hot wallets leaked and the attacker created withdrawals directly, draining Ethereum and Tron hot wallets. No victim signing step.

name: Wintermute
notes: Wintermute gave Optimism the address of its Ethereum Safe, which had never been deployed on Optimism. After 20M OP were sent there, an attacker replayed the Safe deployer's pre-EIP-155 transactions to recreate the ProxyFactory on Optimism and called createProxy until a Safe they controlled landed at that address; no victim signed anything, and 17M OP were later returned.

name: Gravity Bridge
notes: Early reports suspected a validator key compromise, but analyses found a logic flaw: permissionless deployERC20() with an unvalidated _cosmosDenom let the attacker poison the denom-to-ERC20 registry and withdraw real custody tokens (~$5.4M); no stolen key needed. No official post-mortem yet.

name: Mirror
notes: Mirror's lock contract on Terra had no duplicate check in unlock_position_funds, so on Oct 8, 2021 an attacker passed his own position ID many times and drained about $90M of other users' short collateral. Nobody noticed until FatMan disclosed it in May 2022.

name: GANA Payment
notes: The attacker took ownership of GANA's BSC staking contract, which Halborn says was likely done with stolen private keys. They then inflated reward rates and used unstake to drain about $3.1M, laundering it through Tornado Cash. No source describes the owner being tricked into signing.

name: USDGambit and TLP
notes: The single deployer account controlling both projects was taken over (stolen key or hijacked session); the attacker took the proxy admin, deployed a malicious implementation, drained ~$1.5M on Arbitrum, and sent it to Tornado Cash.

name: Slope Wallet
notes: Slope's mobile app sent users' mnemonics in readable form to its centralized Sentry logging server, and attackers used them to drain about 8,000 Solana wallets ($4-5M) in Aug 2022. Seed exposure; victims signed nothing.

name: Patricia
notes: Nigerian app Patricia disclosed in May 2023 a theft of about ₦2B from company crypto wallets, reportedly from a breach in Jan 2022; police charges cite unauthorized alteration of computer systems. Company-side compromise; no user signing.

name: Safemoon
notes: A SafeMoon contract upgrade the day before left the burn function publicly callable. The attacker burned SFM out of the SFM/BNB pair to inflate the price, then sold into it and drained ~$8.9M of BNB (80% was later returned).

name: Monoswap
notes: Attackers posing as VCs got a developer to install a fake 'Kakao' video-call app, an infostealer that took private keys from his machine. They then drained Monoswap's staked liquidity on Blast (~$1.3M).

name: Yala
malicious_action: leaked temporary deployment keys used to wire a malicious OFT into the YU bridge and mint 120M unbacked tokens
notes: The attacker obtained the temporary keys used to deploy Yala's Solana LayerZero OFT in August 2025 and left a dormant backdoor. Forty days later they used it to mint 120M unbacked tokens, bridge them as YU, and cash out about $7.6M.

name: Crypto.com
notes: The attacker bypassed Crypto.com's 2FA and withdrew 4,836 ETH and 444 BTC from 483 custodial user accounts in Jan 2022. Exchange-side authentication failure; no user signing.

name: Bitcurex
malicious_action: about 2,300-2,400 BTC lost from the exchange after an alleged intrusion
notes: Bitcurex said 'external interference' damaged its IT systems on Oct 13, 2016 and part of its assets were lost; the Polish exchange then shut down. The claim was never independently verified and observers questioned it, but there was no human signing step either way.

name: DragonEx
notes: Hackers transferred both platform and user crypto assets out of DragonEx's custody on Mar 24, 2019. Exchange-side compromise; users signed nothing.

name: ZB Exchange
notes: ZB's hot wallet was drained (~$4.3-4.8M) on Aug 1, 2022, which the exchange first announced as a 'sudden failure'; the attacker signed directly.

name: Vulcan Forged
malicious_action: export of 96 custodial wallet keys through Vulcan Forged's Venly credentials, then PYR drained
notes: Attackers compromised Vulcan Forged's own servers, captured user PINs, and used the platform's Venly credentials to export the keys of 96 custodial wallets, draining about $140M in PYR. Users never signed anything.

name: Polygon
notes: Whitehats reported a critical vulnerability in the Polygon PoS genesis MATIC contract. Before the 5 December 2021 emergency hard fork took effect, a malicious hacker used it to steal 801,601 MATIC (~$2M), a loss the foundation covered.

name: ZKsync
malicious_action: compromised airdrop admin key called sweepUnclaimed() to mint unclaimed ZK
notes: An attacker with the private key controlling ZKsync's three airdrop distribution contracts called sweepUnclaimed to mint about $5M of unclaimed ZK tokens. How the key leaked was not disclosed.

name: Samudai
notes: An attacker compromised Samudai DAO's multisig wallets and the founder's personal wallet together and took ~$1.25M ETH. The method is undisclosed; draining the founder's own wallet as well suggests stolen keys (inferred).

name: Mirror
notes: After the Terra collapse, most Terra Classic validators ran an outdated price oracle that valued LUNC at about 5 UST instead of a fraction of a cent. Attackers used near-worthless LUNC to drain Mirror's mAsset pools (~$2M): an oracle failure, with no signing involved.

name: Roll
notes: Private keys for Roll's hot wallet were compromised and ~$5.7M in social tokens drained; Roll said it did not know how the keys were obtained.

name: Picostocks
malicious_action: BTC taken from two separate exchange wallets, including 'cold' storage
notes: About 5,896 BTC was taken from two Picostocks wallets on different machines. The exchange saw no intrusion and suspected the wallet files were copied by people with past system access and then decrypted. Quadriga dates this to late November 2013, not February 2014 as in DeFiLlama.

name: Huobi
malicious_action: HTX hot wallets drained after APT38 backdoored an HTX server
notes: About $12.5-13.6M left HTX's hot wallets on Nov 22, 2023, shortly after the HECO bridge drain. An FBI complaint says an HTX employee ran malware from a fake GitHub repository and APT38 then backdoored an HTX server.

name: Trust Wallet Wallet
notes: The Shai-Hulud npm worm gave attackers Trust Wallet's extension source code and Chrome Web Store API key. They published a malicious v2.68 that sent logged-in users' private keys to an attacker domain (Dec 24-26, 2025), and about $8.5M was stolen from about 2,520 wallets.

name: Harmony Bridge
malicious_action: withdrawals from the 2-of-5 bridge multisig signed with two stolen keys
notes: The Horizon bridge needed only 2 of 5 signatures. Lazarus (per the FBI) got into internal Harmony servers, compromised two keys, and signed the drain transactions themselves, taking about $100M.

name: Coinsecure
malicious_action: BTC moved out of the hot wallet after its private key was exposed
notes: 438 BTC was lost after the hot-wallet private key was exposed while Coinsecure's CSO was extracting Bitcoin Gold for customers. The CEO blamed the CSO, the CSO claimed a hack, and a UN panel later listed it among suspected DPRK attacks. Either way, the key holder or thief signed directly.

name: Defrost
malicious_action: owner key added a fake collateral token and malicious oracle, minted H2O and liquidated vaults
notes: Defrost V1's owner key was used to add a fake collateral token and price oracle, mint 100M H2O and liquidate users (about $12M). The team said the key was stolen; CertiK, PeckShield and De.Fi treated it as an exit scam, and the funds were 'recovered' two days later with no explanation. It is either key theft or a rug, not a deceived signer.

name: Bilaxy
notes: Bilaxy's Ethereum hot wallet was hacked and ~296 tokens (~$21.7M) were withdrawn by the attacker.

name: WazirX: India
malicious_action: Safe delegatecall (operation=1) replacing the multisig's masterCopy/implementation with attacker contract 0xef279c2a…5fc6
notes: WazirX signers using Liminal's custody interface saw routine GALA/USDT transfers, but their signatures (3 WazirX + 1 Liminal) authorised a delegatecall that swapped the Safe's implementation for an attacker contract, which then drained about $235M (Lazarus attributed). The upgrade tx was submitted by the exploiter at 06:17 UTC on 18 Jul 2024, an hour before the drains.

name: Bybit
malicious_action: Safe execTransaction with operation=1 (DELEGATECALL) to attacker contract 0x96221423681A6d52E184D440a8eFCEbB105C7242 calling transfer(0xbDd077f651EBe7f7b3cE16fe5F2b025BE2969516, 0); run in the proxy's storage, it overwrote the Safe masterCopy (slot 0) with a malicious implementation exposing sweepETH/sweepERC20
notes: JavaScript injected into Safe{Wallet}'s AWS-hosted frontend showed the signers of Bybit's cold-wallet Safe (0x1Db92e2EeBC8E0c075a02BeA49a2935BcD2dFCF4) a routine transfer while their Ledgers blind-signed this delegatecall. Raw bytes re-checked over RPC: execTransaction 0x6a761202, value 0, safeTxGas 45746, gasPrice 0, block 21895238. The attacker then used the backdoored implementation to sweep ~401k ETH plus stETH, mETH and cmETH.

name: CrediX
notes: CrediX's own multisig added the attacker as Admin and Bridge in ACLManager six days earlier; the attacker then minted unbacked collateral and borrowed out ~$4.5M. The team promised a refund deal and then vanished, so it is widely suspected to be an exit scam.

name: Florence Finance
malicious_action: 1,456,162 USDC transfer to address-poisoning lookalike 0xB087269D…5870 instead of intended 0xB087cfa7…5870
notes: On 26 Nov 2023 Florence Finance's Safe paid the legitimate 0xB087cfa7…5870. Two days later it sent 1.456M USDC to a poisoned lookalike, 0xB087269D…5870 (tagged Fake_Phishing268386), which shares the same first and last four characters. The transfer did exactly what it encoded.

name: Rubic
notes: Attackers obtained the private key of Rubic's admin wallet (which ran the RBC/BRBC bridge and staking rewards; malware suspected) and sold ~34M RBC/BRBC (~$1.2M). No user contracts were affected.

name: QANplatform
notes: The QANX bridge deployer key was a vanity address made with vanity-eth-gpu, which shares Profanity's weak-seed flaw; the attacker brute-forced the key and drained the bridge (~$2M).

name: AirDAO
notes: An email impersonating a known partner carried a malicious attachment, and through it the attackers gained control of AirDAO's AMB/ETH liquidity position. They drained 41.6M AMB and 126.5 ETH (~$1.05M).

name: Triple-A
notes: Unauthorized access to Triple-A's own treasury hot wallets on seven chains; the attacker kept sweeping new deposits for 31+ hours (~$9.7-11.8M), which means ongoing signing capability, not a one-off approval. Root cause still under investigation.

name: NEKO
notes: Neko Network's lending MainPool (Maze Protocol, BSC) let anyone borrow onBehalfOf any address without a credit-delegation check. Attackers opened loans against other users' collateral and kept the borrowed funds, adding about $4M of debt across 17 victims; about $1.8M was returned.

name: FriesDAO
malicious_action: owner key of a Profanity vanity address brute-forced and contracts drained
notes: FriesDAO's contracts were still owned by an address generated with the flawed Profanity vanity tool, not the multisig the team thought. The attacker recomputed its private key and drained about $2.3M.

name: Coinbin
notes: The South Korean exchange Coinbin (successor to Youbit) filed for bankruptcy with about $26M missing, citing employee embezzlement; a general manager is reported to have deleted or controlled the wallet private keys. The loss came from an insider, not a signing deception. Whether it was deliberate or negligent is disputed.

name: Raydium AMM
notes: A trojan compromised the private key of Raydium's AMM pool-owner account. The attacker used it to inflate SyncNeedTake and call withdraw_pnl, draining ~$4.4M in fees and liquidity from nine pools.

name: ValueDefi
notes: Value DeFi's vStake profit-sharing pool on BSC was missing the 'initialized = true' line in initialize(). On May 5, 2021 the attacker re-initialized it, made himself operator, and called governanceRecoverUnsupported() to drain the vBSWAP/BUSD LP, about $10M.

name: Bitget
notes: Attackers used zero-days in two third-party security appliances to get internal credentials, reached Bitget's production wallet job server, and injected forged withdrawal requests that the automated approval pipeline signed (~$387.5M from hot and warm wallets). Halborn and Mandiant/SlowMist describe no human approver being deceived; the attacker controlled the signing pipeline.

name: Texture
notes: Insufficient access control in Texture's USDC vault program on Solana let an attacker drain ~$2.2M of user funds. They returned $1.98M and kept the rest as a 10% bounty.

name: LiFi Finance
notes: A LI.FI contract facet failed to validate input and allowed arbitrary calls, so the attacker made it call transferFrom against tokens users had approved to it with infinite allowances, draining ~$10M. The users had approved a legitimate contract, and no new victim signature was needed.

name: New Market Trading
notes: New Market Trading's custom Gnosis Safe module (SquidRouterModule, deployed at the same address on Ethereum, Base and Arbitrum) read a 'delegate' address out of attacker-controlled cross-chain payload bytes and trusted it for permission checks. On May 25, 2026 the attacker used this to route swaps through his own Uniswap V3 pools and drained about $3.98M from 88 customer Safes. No owner or delegate key was compromised and no victim signed anything.

name: EtherDelta
notes: Attackers used an EtherDelta employee's phone number to take over their email, then changed DNS to point to a cloned site that collected the private keys users entered and withdrew their funds (Dec 2017). This was phishing that stole keys, not a signed malicious transaction.

name: Exmo
notes: Exmo's hot wallets were drained (~$10.5M) and most funds went to Poloniex; the attacker signed directly.

name: Atomic Wallet
notes: Thousands of users' non-custodial Atomic wallets were emptied (over $35M initially, later estimates higher) by an attacker who already held their private keys. The root cause was never disclosed (theories include compromised infrastructure or BGP hijack), laundering patterns point to Lazarus, and no victim signing step was involved.

name: Meerkat Finance
notes: One day after launch, the Meerkat deployer upgraded two vault proxies to new logic whose only function removed funds to the owner, draining ~13-14M BUSD and ~73k BNB (~$31M). The team first claimed a hack, then deleted its accounts.

name: Atlantis Loans
notes: On 7 June 2023 an attacker created a malicious proposal in Atlantis Loans' GovernorBravo. Once it passed they took control of the contracts and swapped in a backdoored implementation that pulled assets from users who still had approvals (~$1-2.5M): a governance takeover, not signer deception.

name: Audius
notes: Audius's proxy admin slot collided with OpenZeppelin Initializable's storage, so the attacker could re-initialize the Governance, Staking and DelegateManager contracts and give themselves voting power. They then passed and executed a governance proposal moving ~18.5M AUDIO out of the treasury.

name: BTER
malicious_action: 50M NXT taken from BTER's NXT central account after a hosting server was hacked
notes: Attackers hacked one of BTER's hosting servers and stole 50M NXT (about $1.65M) from its NXT central account; BTER admitted fault. The amount and day match the August 15, 2014 NXT theft, so DeFiLlama's 2015 date and Bitcoin chain look wrong.

name: Coincheck
notes: Attackers stole the private key of Coincheck's single-signature NEM hot wallet and moved ~523M XEM (~$534M) out themselves. No human review step existed.

name: BounceBit
notes: An authorization check built into BounceBit Chain's Evmos-based stack did not confirm that the source account had approved a transfer, letting the attacker move ~286.5M BB (~$3M) out of nine accounts in 14 transactions. BounceBit says no keys were compromised and no signatures were forged, and it retired the chain.

name: Drop
notes: Same Neutron governance takeover as Astroport (22 Sep 2026): the passed 'AIATO' proposal used chain-level MsgUpdateAdmin to hand the attacker admin over Drop's liquid-staking contracts, overriding app-level multisigs. The contracts were then migrated and drained.

name: Mozaic
malicious_action: security-module private keys stolen by a team developer and used to move funds out of the vaults
notes: Mozaic says the thief was one of its own developers, who illegally obtained a security module's private keys by compromising a core team member's data and moved over $2M out of the vaults to MEXC and Binance.

name: BNS
notes: 'BNS' is the Indian exchange BitBNS, which lost about $7.5M on Feb 1, 2022 and told users it was 'system maintenance' until ZachXBT exposed it in 2023. The root cause was not disclosed; exchange-wallet compromise is inferred, with no sign of user signing.

name: Volo Vault
malicious_action: compromised privileged operator key used to withdraw from WBTC, XAUm and USDC vaults
notes: GoPlus and ExVul traced the April 2026 drain of three Volo vaults on Sui (about $3.5M) to a privileged operator key compromised through social engineering, not a contract bug; the attacker called vault withdrawal functions directly. No post-mortem has been published yet.

name: DEXX
malicious_action: user wallets drained with private keys leaked from DEXX's custodial key store
notes: DEXX was a trading terminal that held users' private keys. Those keys leaked (SlowMist and others point to DEXX's centralized custody and key-export handling), and about 900 victims lost roughly $21M. The users signed nothing.

name: PolyNetwork
notes: On Aug 12, 2024 Poly Network's CMCC cross-chain contract on Neo N3 was exploited for about $4-5M, emptying the bridge hot wallet (about 20-25% of the backing for Flamingo's f- and p-assets). Flamingo calls it a smart-contract exploit and DefiLlama tags it as reentrancy; I found no detailed post-mortem. This is a different incident from the July 2023 Poly Network consensus-key theft.

name: FinNexus
notes: Someone holding the project's admin private key changed the token owner, minted, and withdrew ~$7M; widely suspected to be an inside job, not a signing deception.

name: AnubisDAO
notes: About 20 hours into the Copper LBP sale, the pool-owner EOA 0x872254d530ae8983628cb1eaafc51f78d78c86d9 exited the Balancer LBP and, in the next block, sent 13,556 WETH to 0x9fc53c75046900d1f58209f50f534852ae9f912a (checked on-chain). It is widely treated as a rug pull, although the person linked to the receiving address claimed a phishing compromise.

name: PancakeSwap
notes: Starting Apr 12, 2021, whoever controlled the PancakeSwap Lottery admin account (0x35f16a...) bought tickets, entered the drawing phase and drew in the same block, which made the block-hash randomness predictable, and won about 59,765 CAKE (about $1.8M) over several draws. SlowMist records it as a leaked admin key, but an insider cannot be ruled out; no user signed anything.

name: BSC TMM/USDT
notes: Using flash loans from several lenders, the attacker caused TMM in the TMM/USDT PancakeSwap pair to be burned to the dead address until the reserve was 1 TMM. They then swapped 850M TMM for ~272M USDT and kept ~1.665M USDT after repaying the loans: a token/pair reserve-logic flaw.

name: Bitfinex
malicious_action: 2,000+ fraudulent BTC withdrawals authorized from inside Bitfinex's network, bypassing BitGo co-signing
notes: Ilya Lichtenstein admitted he hacked Bitfinex's network and fraudulently authorized more than 2,000 withdrawals of about 119,754 BTC, getting around the BitGo approval that was meant to co-sign. Everything was automated; no person reviewed a disguised transaction.

name: TopGoal
notes: Hot wallets operated by TopGoal were compromised, specifically the one distributing TopPrize rewards (~4.8M tokens lost).

name: RRWallet
notes: RRWallet produced seed phrases from CryptoJS's weak RNG (CVE-2026-71851), so attackers could regenerate them and sweep wallets (~$2M). The wallet is discontinued with no fix.

name: UvToken
notes: UvToken's staking pool withdrawal function did not validate user input, so the attacker passed a malicious contract address and used it to drain ~5,011 BNB, later sent to Tornado Cash.

name: Liquid Global
notes: Liquid's hot (warm) wallets were compromised and ~$91M was drained across chains by the attacker signing directly; Liquid moved remaining assets to cold storage.

name: Multichain
malicious_action: funds moved out of Multichain MPC router addresses after a login to the CEO's cloud account
notes: All of Multichain's MPC nodes ran under CEO Zhaojun's personal cloud account. On July 7, 2023, while he was in Chinese police custody, someone logged in from a Kunming IP and moved about $126M out of the MPC addresses. Whether that was police, insiders, or thieves is unknown, but whoever it was held the keys and signed directly, with no signer deceived.

name: BigONE
notes: A supply-chain compromise of BigONE's production network let attackers rewrite the logic of its account and risk-control servers, so the exchange's own hot-wallet system approved about $27M of withdrawals. BigONE/SlowMist say no private keys leaked: the signing infrastructure was abused and no human reviewed the transactions.

name: OpenSea
malicious_action: personal_sign (EIP-191 '\x19Ethereum Signed Message:\n32' prefix) of a legacy Wyvern v2.2 order hash for OpenSea Wyvern Exchange v1 (0x7Be8076f4EA4A4AD08075C2508e481d6C946D12b): a 'blank-check' zero-price sell order that the attacker completed and matched via atomicMatch_ to take the NFTs
notes: During OpenSea's February 2022 contract migration, phishing got 17 users to sign Wyvern orders off-chain. The listed txs are the attacker's (0x3E0DeFb8...7A8A74, Etherscan Fake_Phishing5169) executions matching those orders at price 0 on the v1 exchange; on-chain, all 17 OrdersMatched events in the window are on the v1 exchange, whose source uses the personal_sign prefix. Example: Azuki #3071 and Cool Cats #8992/#434 taken from 0xB8c1fECe...96D4.

name: Indodax
notes: A Lazarus-style intrusion into Indodax's withdrawal infrastructure drained hot wallets across several chains in Sep 2024 (estimates of $15-25M). SlowMist pointed to a compromised withdrawal system rather than a simple key leak; either way the exchange's own systems signed and no user signed anything.

name: Wemix
malicious_action: forged withdrawals made with a stolen NILE internal authentication key
notes: A developer had uploaded an internal authentication key for the NILE NFT platform's monitoring system to a public repository. The attacker used it to forge withdrawal transactions; 13 of 15 attempts succeeded, taking 8.65M WEMIX (about $6.2M).

name: LCX
notes: The private key of LCX's Ethereum hot wallet (0x4631…3e6f) was compromised, and about $7.94M in ETH, USDC and tokens was sent to the attacker on Jan 8, 2022. Custodial key compromise.

name: pNetwork
notes: pNetwork says a leaked private key, plus a misconfiguration at contract creation, let an attacker take over the owner of the pGALA proxyAdmin on BNB Chain (Nov 3, 2022). pNetwork then 'white-hat' minted pGALA and drained about $4.3M from PancakeSwap pools before redeploying; no victim signing.

name: Mt. Gox
notes: In June 2011 a hacker used credentials taken from a Mt. Gox auditor's compromised computer to move a large amount of bitcoin to himself and place a huge nominal sell order that briefly crashed the price. Stolen privileged credentials, not a deceived signer.

name: Ionic Protocol
malicious_action: Comptroller _deployMarket listing attacker's counterfeit LBTC (0x964dd444…fba3) as collateral
notes: After weeks of business-development talks with attackers posing as Lombard Finance, Ionic's admin Safe deployed a market for their fake LBTC on 31 Jan 2025. The transaction did exactly what it encoded. On 4 Feb the attacker minted 250 fake LBTC, posted it as collateral, and borrowed about $8.6M of real assets.

name: Unleash Protocol
notes: Through Unleash's multisig, an external EOA was given admin control; it then upgraded a contract and withdrew ~$3.9M (1,337 ETH to Tornado Cash). Unleash has not said whether signer keys were stolen or signers were tricked into approving the admin change, so this is a candidate for multisig deception that is unconfirmed.

name: BitoPro
notes: About $11.5M was drained from BitoPro's hot wallets on Tron, Ethereum, Solana and Polygon on May 8, 2025, during a wallet-system upgrade. BitoPro attributed the attack to Lazarus (malware, per SlowMist's database); exchange-side compromise with no user signing.

name: IoTeX
notes: An attacker compromised an employee's machine through suspected social engineering, stayed inside for a long time, and used the key that owned the ioTube Validator contract to push a malicious upgrade, draining TokenSafe reserves (~$4.4M) and minting CIOTX.

name: One Ring Finance
notes: A flash-loan attack manipulated OneRing's vault share-price calculation and withdrew ~1.45M USDC. The exploit tx is on Fantom, not Ethereum as listed here.

name: Gate
malicious_action: withdrawals from Gate.io wallets using private keys stolen via malware
notes: A US DOJ forfeiture complaint (Gate.io is 'Exchange 1') says an employee downloaded malware from a fake 'potential client', which gave North Korean hackers remote access and the exchange's private keys; about $230M was stolen. Gate.io never publicly confirmed the hack.

name: Fortress Trust
notes: The cloud tools of a Fortress Trust third-party analytics vendor were compromised, and the access was used to take $12-15M (mostly BTC) from customer accounts in Sep 2023; Ripple made customers whole. Credential/infrastructure compromise; no victim signing.

name: AFX Bridge
malicious_action: 24.15M USDC bridge withdrawal signed with 5 of 7 stolen hot-validator keys
notes: AFX's post-mortem says a developer contacted on Telegram cloned a malicious repository. From that workstation the attacker pivoted through JFrog into AFX's infrastructure, took five of seven bridge validator keys (enough for the >2/3 quorum), and signed a 24.15M USDC withdrawal themselves.

name: Truflation
notes: Malware, believed to have been planted on a team computer around Token2049, collected enough private keys to drain Truflation's treasury multisig and personal wallets (~$5.2M) across eight chains.

name: CoinPoker
malicious_action: about $2M USDT moved out of the hot wallet on BNB Chain, Ethereum and Polygon
notes: An unauthorized address took control of CoinPoker's custodian-managed hot wallet on Nov 7, 2024 and moved about $2M, laundering it through Tornado Cash. The cause was described as a third-party vulnerability; no human signer was involved.

name: KuCoin
notes: Private keys of KuCoin's BTC/ERC-20 hot wallets were exposed and the attacker withdrew ~$281M directly; attributed to Lazarus. No signer was tricked.

name: US Government Crypto Wallet
malicious_action: about $20M moved out of a USMS-controlled wallet holding seized Bitfinex-hack funds
notes: In October 2024 about $20M of seized Bitfinex-hack funds left a US-government wallet; most came back within a day. ZachXBT and TRM later traced the funds to John 'Lick' Daghita, son of the president of USMS crypto-custody contractor CMDSS, who was arrested in March 2026. How he got key access has not been made public.

name: SUPERFORTUNE AI
malicious_action: Safe execTransaction (delegatecall to MultiSendCallOnly) transferring 14,980,736.643 GUA to vanity lookalike 0x70AE678b...5C15 instead of airdrop claim contract 0x70ae7D3D...5c15
notes: The team's 3-of-5 Safe v1.4.1 on BNB Chain (0x39831ebc3f2b022cf8791457f65d12275922a15d; BNB Chain, not Ethereum) signed and executed a MultiSendCallOnly batch that sent 14,980,736.643 GUA, meant for the airdrop claim contract 0x70ae7D3DECfB4C3aE996fb1c07092566F73D5c15, to the vanity lookalike 0x70AE678b457C5E1b3fD7AD9537F234dFc1795C15; the attacker dumped it for ~2,784 ETH. The signed bytes contain the lookalike, so a full-address decode would have exposed it, but the root cause (substituted input or tooling vs a compromised UI showing the real address, which would make this SIGNING_DECEPTION_MULTISIG) is unconfirmed; the hash comes from BNB Chain RPC data (GUA Transfer log plus decoded execTransaction), not from a published post-mortem.

name: Multichain
malicious_action: MPC router private key derived from a reused ECDSA nonce, then V3 pools drained
notes: Two Anyswap V3 router transactions on BSC were signed with the same ECDSA R value (nonce). That let the attacker compute the MPC account's private key and drain about $7.9M in USDC and MIM.

name: INX Digital Company
notes: A malicious actor breached the servers of a third-party vendor that served an INX subsidiary and executed unauthorized trades, costing about $1.6M (Dec 20, 2023). Vendor credential/infrastructure compromise; no victim signing.

name: OlaXBT
notes: Attackers gained control of a BSC multisig holding 32M AIO, reportedly after a developer's device was compromised through phishing, and sold the tokens for about $2M. Sources call it a private-key compromise. DeFiLlama labels it 'Signer Phishing', but no source says signers approved a disguised transaction.

name: LND
notes: LNDfi, an Aave V3 fork on Sonic and HyperEVM, says a developer it unknowingly hired, later identified as a DPRK IT worker (ZachXBT helped attribute it), took the project's admin keys. Forty-one days earlier the deployer had added a Pool Admin bypass to onlyPool, and on May 9, 2025 the Pool Admin called transferUnderlyingTo to drain about $1.18M. This was a privileged insider, not a deceived signer.

name: LianGoPay
notes: The LGTPool owner/admin created a fake LP staking pool (Pool #3), then large amounts of fake LP were staked in it to mint 6.14M LGT in rewards (~$1.6M). This abuse of admin privilege is treated as a rug pull.

name: Bondly
notes: According to Bondly, the attacker got into the CEO's password-manager account, which held his hardware wallet's seed phrase. With the owner keys they moved and minted about 373M BONDLY and sold it.

name: Bitrue
notes: Bitrue reported a 'brief exploit in one of our hot wallets' that let the attacker withdraw ~$23M; a hot-wallet key/server compromise with no human signer.

name: Swerve
malicious_action: Governance proposal to transfer the ~$1.3M DAI/USDC/USDT pool's assets to the attacker
notes: In March 2023, an attacker built up SWRV voting power (450k across two addresses) in the abandoned, community-run Swerve DAO and pushed proposals to take the stablecoin pool's ~$1.3M. Halborn reported the vote still short of passing, while ChainCatcher/The Block reported ~$1.3M lost; whether funds actually left is unconfirmed.

name: SwissBorg
malicious_action: 8 hidden stake Authorize instructions reassigning stake-account withdraw authority to the attacker, embedded in a routine ~975 SOL deactivate/unstake transaction
notes: Using a Kiln engineer's stolen GitHub token, the attacker reached Kiln's infrastructure and patched the Kiln Connect API to return a malicious unstake transaction for holders of more than 150k SOL. On Aug 31, 2025 a quorum of signatories in SwissBorg's custody solution approved that transaction (an MPC/custody quorum, not an on-chain multisig), which handed withdraw authority over about 193k SOL to the attacker, who withdrew it on Sep 8. The hash is the Aug 31 transaction SwissBorg signed (also listed by QuillAudits as the 'setup' tx).

name: pcash
notes: The EOS project PayCash ('pcash', contracts swap.pcash and token.pcash) lost about $2M in May 2023, and SlowMist lists the method as unknown. The attacker account's on-chain history (via a Hyperion API) shows it deploying its own contract and repeatedly triggering 'deposit refund' payouts of USDT and MLNK from the pcash contracts. That points to a deposit/refund logic flaw rather than a stolen key or a victim signature, but this is my inference.

name: EasyFi
notes: The attacker had persistent access to EasyFi's dedicated admin machine and injected a malicious MetaMask build that stole the admin private keys and mnemonic. They later moved the admin-wallet funds themselves.

name: Meteora DAMM V2
malicious_action: ~$1.5M USDC sent into a fraudulent OTC escrow controlled by scammers posing as a counterparty in a MET buyback
notes: While trying to buy back MET over the counter, Meteora's team was deceived by a fake escrow setup and lost $1.5M USDC, disclosed in its Q1 2026 Token Holder Report; it was not a smart-contract exploit. No transaction hash appears in the sources that could be read, and the Solana payload format is inferred from the chain listing.

name: Ribbon
notes: An Aevo update to the oracle code used by legacy Ribbon DOV vaults introduced a precision mismatch and an access-control flaw. The attacker forged oracle price updates and created options products that expired with excessive payouts, taking ~$2.7M; sources describe a bug in the team's own upgrade, not key theft or signer deception.

name: Rocket Pool
malicious_action: approve(0x1661F1B207629e4F385DA89cFF535C8E5Eb23Ee3, 171,795.85 RPL) on the RPL token, twice the victim's balance, to a drainer EOA that Etherscan flags as Fake_Phishing66321
notes: This was the phishing of POAP founder Patricio Worthalter (poap.eth), not a Rocket Pool protocol breach. Within two blocks of his approval, drainer transferFrom calls (0xc3a9d6e4...819b, 0x13cd0edd...f632) took 85,898 RPL (~$3.8M), split 64,423 / 21,474 between two addresses.

name: Radix
notes: A Radix Engine defect introduced in June 2023 let a transaction hand any vault's internal address to custom package code and withdraw from it without the owner's authorisation. On Aug 31, 2026 the attacker took about $1.26M in 26 transactions and bridged it out via Hyperlane; validators halted the network for about 10 days. No user keys or signatures were involved.

name: Zaif
malicious_action: unauthorized transfers from the hot-wallet server (BTC, BCH, MONA)
notes: Attackers had access to Zaif's hot-wallet server for about two hours on Sept 14, 2018 and moved out about 6.7B yen in BTC, BCH and MonaCoin. The exchange only noticed three days later.

name: Pike V1
notes: After the Apr 26 CCTP exploit, Pike pushed an upgrade to pause the protocol that changed the storage layout and moved the 'initialized' variable. On Apr 30, 2024 an attacker called initialize on the spoke contracts, took ownership and used upgradeToAndCall to install a malicious implementation, draining about $1.6M in ETH, ARB and OP without any admin key.

name: Wintermute
notes: Wintermute's hot-wallet vanity address came from Profanity, whose 32-bit seed let the attacker brute-force the private key; that key was still a vault admin and was used to drain about $160M. This was not phishing, whatever the label says.

name: Token of Power
notes: The attacker bought just over half of TOP's 16,384-token supply. Because the Aragon DAO had no timelock, they created, voted on and executed a proposal in one transaction that minted 10B TOP and drained about 944 WETH from the Balancer pool.

name: Dego Finance
malicious_action: team liquidity addresses drained and minting contract hijacked
notes: Dego says the keys of team addresses holding DEGO and its Uniswap/PancakeSwap liquidity were compromised. The attacker pulled the liquidity and minted about 1.18M DEGO through the hijacked minting contract, taking about $10M across ETH, BSC and Cronos.

name: Tether
malicious_action: USDT moved from the Tether treasury wallet to an unauthorized bitcoin address
notes: Tether said $30.95M USDT was removed from its treasury wallet on Nov 19, 2017 'through malicious action by an external attacker', and it froze the tokens with a software update. The treasury wallet was reportedly protected by a single private key; the exact compromise path was never disclosed.

name: Inputs.io
notes: Attackers compromised Inputs.io's hosting account (through old, easily reset email accounts and a host-side MFA failure) and stole 4,100 BTC from its online wallets on Oct 23 and 26, 2013. Custodial key compromise.

name: Astra Nova
malicious_action: about 860M RVV dumped from a compromised third-party market-maker account
notes: Astra Nova said one of its third-party market maker's accounts was compromised and about 860M RVV (8.6% of supply) was sold for about $10M. Analysts questioned that story and some users suspect insider theft.

name: CoinSpot
malicious_action: 1,262 ETH moved out of a CoinSpot hot wallet
notes: ZachXBT flagged 1,262 ETH (about $2.4M) leaving a known CoinSpot hot wallet on Nov 8, 2023; CertiK called it a probable private-key compromise. CoinSpot gave no root cause.

name: TSD (True Seigniorage Dollar)
notes: An attacker cheaply built up about 33% of TSD DAO voting power (the developer held 9%), then proposed and voted through an implementation that added mint code. They minted about 11.8B TSD for themselves and dumped it on PancakeSwap.

name: Kronos Research
notes: The attacker stole Kronos Research's API keys and used them to drain about $26M from the trading firm's wallets in Nov 2023. Credential theft; no victim signing.

name: SecondFi
notes: An app update shipped June 8, 2026 derived signature nonces only from the transaction hash, so attackers could compute private keys from public signatures and sweep SecondFi users' Cardano wallets (~$2.4M confirmed; SlowMist estimated much more at risk).

name: Bitcoin Mission
notes: Blockaid flagged multiple malicious transactions against Bitcoin Mission's contracts (@btcmapp, 'BTCM') on Arbitrum, draining over $1M, and BlockThreat classifies it as a contract logic error. Few details were published, and nothing points to key theft or signer deception.

name: Platypus Finance
notes: A flash-loan attack on Platypus's new USP stablecoin: emergencyWithdraw() checked solvency without counting borrowed USP. The attacker borrowed USP against flash-loaned collateral, withdrew the collateral and dumped the USP, about $8.5M.

name: Ekubo
notes: A calldata-parsing bug in Ekubo's immutable, unaudited Huff routers on Ethereum and Arbitrum let a caller append bytes that set who transferFrom pulls from, so the attacker spent other addresses' standing approvals, about $1.42M from 31 addresses. About 98% came from one address with an unlimited (max-uint256) WBTC approval to the V2 router; Ekubo says finite approvals were whitehatted out and only infinite approvals remain exposed.

name: NiceHash
notes: NiceHash said its payment system was compromised and the contents of its Bitcoin wallet (about 4,700 BTC) were moved to an attacker address in Dec 2017. Custodial hot-wallet breach; users signed nothing.

name: Steadefi
malicious_action: stolen deployer hot-wallet key used to transfer vault ownership, approve attacker as borrower and drain lending vaults
notes: The UN panel says a fake investor on Telegram sent a Steadefi employee a malicious 'fund presentation', and the employee's MetaMask seed phrase was copied. That exposed the deployer hot wallet that owned every vault, which the attacker used to make themselves an approved borrower and drain about $1.1M.

name: BitGrail
notes: Roughly $170-195M of Nano (XRB) vanished from the Italian exchange BitGrail; the Nano team found no ledger double-spend and blamed BitGrail's own software, while later reporting says most coins left cold wallets and points to a probable inside job (the founder faced fraud charges). The vector is contested (exchange software flaw vs insider), but no signer was deceived either way.

name: Nexus Mutual
malicious_action: NXM transfer of 370,000 NXM to attacker address 0xAd6A4Ace6dcc21c93ca9dbC8a21c7d3a726C1FB1, presented by a tampered MetaMask as a different transaction
notes: An attacker with remote access to founder Hugh Karp's computer replaced his MetaMask extension with a modified one. Karp approved on his hardware wallet what he believed was a routine transaction (claiming rewards); it was actually NXM.transfer to the attacker, verified on Etherscan as sent from twiddle.eth on Dec 14, 2020 09:40 UTC. Halborn's hash 0xfb77… is the attacker's later wNXM move, not the transaction Karp signed.

name: Phemex
notes: Hot wallets on ~16 chains were drained (~$70-85M) at once. Halborn attributes it to likely compromised hot-wallet private keys (Lazarus suspected); no human signer involved.

name: 2gether
notes: Hackers stole 114 BTC and 276 ETH (about €1.18M) from 2gether's systems in Jul/Aug 2020. Spanish police later said an employee's computer, infected with malware hidden in a pirated movie, gave the attackers access.

name: Curio
notes: The attacker bought a small amount of CGT, locked it in Curio's DSChief (a MakerDAO fork), voted his own contract in as the hat (lift), then plotted and executed it through DSPause with no delay. The delegatecalled spell minted about 1B CGT, which he dumped for about $16M. No signer was deceived; Curio calls it a voting-power access-control flaw.

name: Exactly
notes: Exactly's DebtManager periphery contract trusted a caller-supplied market address. The attacker passed a fake market to bypass the permission check and set the victim as _msgSender, then re-entered crossDeleverage to steal depositors' collateral (~$7M).

name: Drift Trade
malicious_action: Pre-signed durable-nonce Squads transactions that created, approved and executed a vault transaction calling Drift UpdateAdmin to an attacker address
notes: DPRK-linked attackers socially engineered 2 of the 5 Drift Security Council signers (a 2-of-5 Squads multisig with zero timelock) into pre-signing durable-nonce transactions that looked routine but hid an admin transfer. On April 1, 2026 they submitted the two signed transactions four slots apart, took Drift admin control, listed a fake collateral token (CVT) and drained about $285M. The program had no bug.

name: HyperVault
notes: HyperVault's team used a privileged onlyHV backdoor to drain nine vaults (~$3.6M) on HyperEVM. They bridged the funds to Ethereum, laundered them through Tornado Cash, and deleted their online presence.

name: Trinity Wallet
notes: The attacker abused Trinity's MoonPay integration, which loaded third-party code from a CDN, to run malicious code inside the wallet and steal users' seeds, then drained about $2M of IOTA (Feb 2020). Seed exfiltration via a supply-chain component; victims signed nothing.

name: Bithumb
notes: Bithumb's hot wallet was hacked overnight on June 19-20, 2018 (about $30M, including XRP). Custodial hot-wallet key compromise.

name: BtcTurk
notes: Attackers got access to the private keys of BtcTurk's hot wallets and drained ~$48-54M across seven chains, repeating the June 2024 incident. Exact access method undisclosed; no human signer step.

name: BitPoint
notes: Unauthorized access to BitPoint's hot wallets drained about 3.5B yen of BTC, XRP, LTC, ETH and BCH in July 2019; cold wallets were not affected. Custodial key compromise.

name: Astroport
notes: On 22 Sep 2026 an attacker bought about 31.6M NTRN minutes before the tally and passed Neutron proposal 'AIATO: AI Agent Takeover', disguised as AI research, whose MsgUpdateAdmin messages gave them admin of ten Astroport and Drop contracts. The contracts were migrated to malicious code and drained within minutes (~$9.4M across both protocols).

name: Bittensor
notes: A malicious bittensor 6.12.2 package uploaded to PyPI stole users' decrypted coldkeys during stake and transfer operations, and the attacker drained ~32,000 TAO (~$8M) from those wallets.

name: Poly Network
notes: The attacker sent a crafted cross-chain message through EthCrossChainManager.verifyHeaderAndExecuteTx that reached EthCrossChainData.putCurEpochConPubKeyBytes, swapping the keeper public key for their own, then authorised withdrawals of ~$611M as the new keeper. A cross-contract logic flaw, not a stolen key; most funds were later returned.

name: Humanity
notes: Root-level malware on a developer's laptop stole seven keys: a hot wallet key plus enough signer keys for the ETH and BSC Safes. The attacker built the Safe transactions offline (bridge upgrade, mint authorization) and signed them; no legitimate signer approved anything.

name: HTX
notes: HTX's hot wallet was compromised and ~5,000 ETH (~$8M) withdrawn; the attacker later returned it for a white-hat bounty.

name: RetoSwap
notes: Two exploits hit the Haveno P2P protocol RetoSwap runs on: on 20 May 2026 forged arbitrator acknowledgement messages redirected multisig escrow to the attacker (~7,000 XMR, ~$2.7M), and on 16 Jun 2026 a dispute-resolution flaw let a buyer release XMR without sending BTC. Both were protocol flaws, not governance proposals; the batch's amount fits the May event and its date fits the June one.

name: CoinEx
notes: CoinEx initially attributed the ~$55-70M multi-chain drain to leaked hot-wallet private keys; Elliptic and Chainalysis linked it to North Korea (Lazarus).

name: Abracadabra Spell
notes: A logic flaw in deprecated V4 Cauldrons on Ethereum let the attacker bypass the insolvency check and mint/borrow 1.79M MIM without backing. The DAO treasury bought the MIM back from the market.

name: Mixin Network
notes: Attackers compromised the database of Mixin's cloud service provider, which gave them access to the network's hot wallets, and drained about $200M. Custodial infrastructure breach; no user signed anything.

name: Banana Gun
notes: A vulnerability in the Telegram message oracle used by the Banana Gun trading bot let the attacker manually transfer about $3M out of 11 users' bot-custodied ETH and SOL wallets (Sep 2024). The bot holds users' keys, so the attacker effectively controlled signing and users signed nothing.

name: swapX
notes: The unverified swapX implementation on BSC exposed a function (0x4f1f05bc) without access control. The attacker used it to spend tokens users had approved to the contract (~$1M): abuse of prior approvals, with no new victim signature.

name: MetaWin
