notes: The attacker exploited a vulnerability in MetaWin's off-chain 'frictionless withdrawal system' to drain about $4M from its ETH and SOL hot wallets. Details were not published, so a withdrawal-logic flaw versus hot-wallet compromise is unclear; either way no victim signature was involved.

name: BingX
notes: Unauthorized access to BingX hot wallets on several chains (~$43-52M); Halborn infers centrally stored hot-wallet keys were stolen. No deceived signer.

name: Ronin Bridge
malicious_action: forged bridge withdrawals signed with 5 of 9 stolen validator keys (173,600 ETH + 25.5M USDC)
notes: Lazarus sent a Sky Mavis engineer a fake job offer whose document carried malware, took over four Sky Mavis validator keys, and got the fifth (Axie DAO) signature through a forgotten gas-free RPC allowlist. The attacker then signed two withdrawals themselves; no human approval step was involved.

name: Ostium
notes: Off-chain pricing infrastructure was breached: the attacker held an authorized oracle-signer key and a PriceUpKeep forwarder role, signed fake BTC price reports, and looped trades to drain 23.75M USDC from the OLP vault. Post-mortem found no contract bug and no multisig compromise.

name: DAO Maker Vesting
notes: On Aug 12, 2021, per DAO Maker's announcement (summarized by SlowMist), an attacker used a DAO Maker wallet to gain administrator rights and drained about $7M in USDC deposits from 5,251 users in 16 transactions. SlowMist and DefiLlama record it as a leaked or compromised private key, and no technical post-mortem was published. This is separate from the Sept 2021 init()/emergencyExit vesting-contract bug.

name: MangoFarmSol
notes: MangoFarm, a Solana farming project, took ~$2M of user deposits and its X account went offline; it is classed as a suspected rug pull.

name: Punk Protocol
notes: Punk Protocol's CompoundModel initialize() was missing its initializer modifier, so the attacker re-initialized each model with his own contract as the forge and called withdrawToForge to pull about $8.9M in USDC, USDT and DAI. A whitehat front-ran part of the attack and about $4.95M was recovered.

name: Transit Finance
notes: Attackers exploited historical vulnerabilities in a legacy Transit Finance TRON contract, deprecated since 2022, taking ~$1.88M from users who had interacted with it; the funds ended up as DAI on Ethereum. A contract bug; Transit promised full compensation.

name: Binance
notes: Attackers harvested user API keys and 2FA codes (phishing, viruses) and submitted withdrawals that passed Binance's checks, taking 7,074 BTC from the hot wallet in one transaction. The phishing stole credentials; nobody was tricked into signing a transaction.

name: Seneca
notes: Seneca's Chamber contracts let anyone pass arbitrary calldata through performOperations (OPERATION_CALL). The attacker used this to call transferFrom on tokens users had approved to the Chamber and took about $6.4M in LSTs and PTs (about 80% was later returned). The losses came from approvals larger than what users had deposited; on-chain, the example victim in the DeFiHackLabs PoC had an unlimited (max-uint256) allowance.

name: Crema Finance
notes: Crema's concentrated-liquidity AMM on Solana did not properly check who owned the tick-data account. The attacker passed in a fake tick account and used flash loans to claim about $8.8M in fees he was never owed. Most of the funds were returned in exchange for a bounty.

name: Bitstamp
notes: After a run of targeted phishing, an employee opened a malicious file that let attackers obtain the hot-wallet server's wallet.dat and passphrase. They then stole ~19,000 BTC from Bitstamp's operational hot wallets in January 2015.

name: WOO X
notes: A targeted phishing attack compromised a team member's device and gave the attacker access to WOO X's development environment. From there the attacker made malicious withdrawals for nine user accounts, paid out of the exchange hot wallets (~$14M across BTC, ETH, BSC and Arbitrum).

name: Zilliqa
notes: A flaw in Zilliqa's Ledger app present since 2019 produced weak Schnorr nonces, letting attackers rebuild private keys from on-chain signatures (accounts with about five or more signed transactions). ZIL was stolen from an exchange partner's cold wallet and native transactions were halted.

name: Polymarket International
malicious_action: EIP-712 authorization, executed through Polymarket's gasless relayer, that moved victims' pUSD to attacker wallets
notes: On June 25, 2026 a compromised third-party marketing script loaded by polymarket.com was replaced at its source with an 18KB drainer that targeted wallets holding more than $100k. It kept prompting victims until they signed an EIP-712 authorization, which was submitted through Polymarket's own relayer, draining about $3M pUSD from 11 wallets (later swapped and bridged into about 1,893 ETH). No source published a victim transaction hash.

name: Step Finance
malicious_action: stake account staker and withdrawer authority reassigned to the attacker, then 261,854 SOL withdrawn
notes: Step says about $40M left its treasury after its executives' devices were compromised (reportedly malware delivered through a fake investor call). The theft is a single-signature stake Authorize transaction from the treasury keypair, which the attacker had rehearsed from their own wallets the day before. That points to the attacker signing with the stolen key, though Step has not said so explicitly.

name: Rikkei Finance
notes: Rikkei's oracle-setting function lacked access control, so the attacker pointed the price oracle at a malicious contract. They inflated their collateral value and borrowed out ~2,671 BNB (~$1.1M).

name: uniBTC
notes: Bedrock's uniBTC vault minted uniBTC 1:1 for native ETH as if ETH were BTC, and the attacker minted uniBTC with ETH and swapped it out (~$2M). This was a contract bug, not malware or social engineering.

name: Yapizon
malicious_action: 3,831 BTC taken from the exchange's hot wallets
notes: The Korean exchange Yapizon (later Youbit) lost 3,831 BTC from its hot wallets on April 22, 2017; South Korean authorities reportedly blamed North Korea. A second hack in December 2017 bankrupted it.

name: FTX
notes: Hours after FTX's bankruptcy filing on 11-12 Nov 2022, roughly $477M left FTX wallets in 'unauthorized transactions'. In 2024 the DOJ charged a SIM-swap ring that Bloomberg's sources identified as the FTX thieves; the attacker moved the funds directly and no FTX signer was tricked into approving anything.

name: MERLIN DEX
notes: During its MAGE liquidity-generation event, the Feeto address, which held max approvals over the pools from deployment, drained ~$1.8M to 0x2744d62a1e9ab975f4d77fe52e16206464ea79b7 and bridged it to Ethereum. Merlin blamed its own back-end developers.

name: IRA Financial / Gemini
notes: Hackers gained control of IRA Financial's master key/account on Gemini (an API-level path that bypassed 2FA and whitelists, per IRA's lawsuit) and withdrew about $36M from client accounts on Feb 8, 2022. Credential compromise; no victim signing.

name: DeltaPrime
notes: DeltaPrime's post-mortem says a misconfiguration let the attacker move ownership of 13 users' Prime Accounts to himself on July 23, 2024, repay their loans and withdraw their collateral, about $1M (290 ETH); $900K came back in exchange for a $100K bounty. This is separate from DeltaPrime's Sept 2024 admin-key compromise and Nov 2024 input-validation exploit.

name: ForceBridge
notes: In April 2025 a tampered upgrade script deployed a malicious Docker image to Force Bridge validator nodes, which exfiltrated three validator private keys. The attacker later used those keys to sign unlocks draining ~$3.7M on Ethereum and BSC: supply-chain key theft by someone the investigation traced to a narrow set with internal access, with no deceived signer.

name: UXLINK
notes: UXLINK's own review (summarized by SlowMist) and Halborn say the attacker spent months posing as a business partner, used deepfake video calls to get into the personal devices of several Safe key holders, and stole their passwords and private keys. With those keys he signed a Safe delegatecall that removed the owners and added himself, drained about $11M from the treasury and minted billions of UXLINK. No signer was tricked into approving a disguised transaction.

name: Fortress Loans
malicious_action: Malicious proposal, passed with purchased FTS votes after an unchallenged 3-day vote, listing FTS as collateral with factor 700000000000000000 (0.7)
notes: The attacker bought enough FTS to pass a proposal making FTS usable as collateral. They then used the price oracle's publicly callable submit() to inflate FTS and borrowed out ~$3M against 100 FTS.

name: SBI Crypto
notes: ZachXBT flagged ~$21M of 'suspicious outflows' across several chains from SBI Group's mining subsidiary, laundered via instant exchanges and Tornado Cash in a North Korea-like pattern. Root cause undisclosed; multi-chain hot-wallet outflows point to key or server compromise (inferred).

name: Aeternity
notes: Not a key compromise: in December 2020 a 51% hashpower (chain-rollback) attack double-spent AE deposits against exchanges such as Gate.io, OKEx and Huobi. Filed under CONTRACT_OR_PROTOCOL_BUG as the nearest consensus-level, no-signature category.

name: Limit Break Payment Processor
notes: Limit Break's unpausable Payment Processor V2, used by Magic Eden in 2024, trusted a sender address relayed by an approved ERC-2771-style forwarder, and that address could be forged. The attacker created zero-price 'sales' of other people's NFTs and drained ~660 WETH through stale approvals (whitehats rescued 23,155 NFTs); victims' old approvals were legitimate and no new signatures were needed.

name: Rain
malicious_action: hot ('send') wallets drained through Rain's BitGo-managed infrastructure using stolen credentials
notes: An FBI forfeiture complaint says a Rain employee was approached on LinkedIn with a fake job and a malicious coding challenge (TraderTraitor malware). The malware stole private keys and credentials for Rain's BitGo-managed infrastructure, and the attackers drained about $16M from its hot wallets.

name: Bancor V3
malicious_action: compromised contract-upgrade wallet withdrew ETH from the BNT converter and took NPXS/BNT
notes: This is Bancor's July 2018 hack, not v3. A wallet used to upgrade Bancor's smart contracts was compromised and used to withdraw 24,984 ETH plus NPXS and BNT (about $23.5M); Bancor froze the BNT.

name: Gamee
notes: The attacker exploited a weakness in GAMEE's GitLab, found the Polygon deployer private key in an old repository, and used it to call recoverERC721s and take about 600M GMEE (about $7M). Leaked key.

name: Fogo Foundation
malicious_action: 400M FOGO moved out of a Foundation wallet
notes: An unidentified actor 'compromised' a Fogo Foundation wallet and moved 400M FOGO (about $3M) to an outside address on Aug 28-29, 2026, and Fogo halted its mainnet. The Foundation has not disclosed the attack path, so stolen key versus tricked signer cannot be determined.

name: Upbit
malicious_action: 342,000 ETH moved out of Upbit's Ethereum hot wallet
notes: On Nov 27, 2019, 342,000 ETH left Upbit's hot wallet. In 2024 Korean police attributed the theft to Lazarus and Andariel but kept the method confidential.

name: XT Exchange
notes: About $1.7M in twelve tokens was taken from XT's platform wallet and converted to ~461.6 ETH. Neither source gives a cause; a hot-wallet compromise is inferred.

name: Bitmart
notes: Hackers used a compromised private key to drain two BitMart hot wallets (Ethereum and BSC, ~$150-196M), then swapped through 1inch and Tornado Cash.

name: SquidRouterModule
notes: This is the same exploit as New Market Trading (id 549): a third-party Safe module named SquidRouterModule, not built by Squid, trusted a delegate address decoded from attacker-supplied payload bytes, letting the attacker drain customer Safes (early reports said about $3.2M on Ethereum and Base). The batch date of 2026-05-04 looks wrong; sources put it on May 25-27, 2026.

name: CoinStats
notes: CoinStats said an employee was socially engineered, which let attackers into its AWS infrastructure, from where they drained 1,590 CoinStats-managed wallets (~$2M). The incident happened on June 22, 2024; DeFiLlama dates it July 12.

name: General Bytes
notes: The attacker uploaded a Java application through General Bytes' master service interface, ran it on the servers, and got access to the database, credentials, and hot-wallet and exchange API keys, stealing about 56 BTC ($1.5M) from operators in March 2023. Server compromise; no victim signing.

name: Matcha
notes: An arbitrary-call bug in the SwapNet router used by Matcha Meta let the attacker transferFrom tokens that about 20 users had approved directly to SwapNet after turning off 0x One-Time Approvals ($13.43M confirmed, one user lost about $13.34M). Existing approvals were abused; no new malicious signature was requested, despite DeFiLlama's 'frontend compromise' label.

name: Upbit
notes: On 27 Nov 2025 automated scripts drained about 44.5B KRW of Solana-network assets from an Upbit hot wallet. Upbit later disclosed a wallet-signing flaw that could let attackers derive private keys from on-chain signatures, and Lazarus is suspected; the attacker signed with the hot-wallet keys.

name: Nobitex
notes: The pro-Israel group Predatory Sparrow broke into Nobitex's internal systems, where hot-wallet private keys were stored insecurely, and sent the funds to unspendable vanity 'burn' addresses on several chains. The attacker held the keys, so there was no signer to deceive.

name: Eterbase
malicious_action: hot wallets drained (ETH, ERC-20s, TRX, XTZ, BTC, ALGO, XRP)
notes: Hackers broke into the Slovak exchange Eterbase in September 2020 and emptied hot wallets on several chains (about $5.4M). Slovak police later told Binance the thieves were Lazarus; the exchange went bankrupt.

name: Starstream Finance
notes: Attackers called the unprotected external execute() function of Starstream's DistributorTreasury contract (on Metis) to siphon STARS, then borrowed ~$8.2M against it on Agora. DeFiLlama labels this a rug pull, but SlowMist attributes it to the contract flaw.

name: Dolomite
notes: A flaw in Dolomite's retired 2019 Ethereum contracts (callFunction in DolomiteMarginProtocol) let the attacker spend approvals that about 187 old users still had on the transfer proxy 0xe2466deb..., taking about $1.8M in USDC, DAI and WETH (about 90% was recovered). On-chain checks of sampled victims show max-uint256 or near-max allowances, so the losses came from unlimited approvals that were never revoked.

name: DODO AMM
notes: DODO V2 Crowdpooling's init() could be called more than once. The attacker initialized pools with a counterfeit token, synced the reserve to zero, re-initialized with the real token and flash-loaned the real tokens out, about $3.8M across the WSZO, WCRES, ETHA and FUSI pools. Front-running bots took part of it and returned most.

name: Kraken
notes: On 2 June 2019 Kraken's illiquid BTC/CAD book flash-crashed from ~C$11,200 to ~C$100. The only explanation offered (by a trader, repeated by SlowMist, never confirmed by Kraken) is that a hacker took over a whale account holding 1,200 BTC (~$10.45M) and dumped it into their own low bids; if true that is account/credential theft, not signing deception.

name: StablR
malicious_action: stolen signer key on a 1-of-3 Safe used to add the attacker as owner, remove the others and mint unbacked USDR/EURR
notes: StablR's minting multisig needed only 1 of 3 signatures, so one compromised signer key let the attacker take over the Safe and mint about $13.5M of unbacked USDR and EURR, netting about $2.8M. No other signer had to approve anything.

name: GERA
notes: After the private key leaked, hackers moved ownership of the GERA token deployer to their own address (0x510E4d61663bE6a24D600AaF90F892dd8c8C61dC) and minted/stole ~$1.48M.

name: BXH
notes: SlowMist records the ~$139M drain of BXH's BSC deployment as private key leakage: the attacker held a privileged key and used it directly. No sign of a deceived signer.

name: Radiant V2
malicious_action: Safe execTransaction calling transferOwnership of LendingPoolAddressesProvider to attacker contract 0x57ba8957…bf5, which then upgraded the LendingPool and drained it
notes: Malware on three developers' machines showed legitimate transactions in the Safe UI while sending a different payload to their Ledger and Trezor devices (3-of-11 Safe), harvesting signatures across apparently 'failed' resubmissions. The attacker executed the signed transferOwnership atomically with a pool upgrade and drain (~$50M); both txs were decoded on-chain to confirm the embedded Safe execTransaction and transferOwnership calldata.

name: Deribit
notes: About $28M was stolen from Deribit's hot wallet by an attacker with access to its keys; cold storage was unaffected.

name: Floating Point Group
notes: FPG reported a June 11, 2023 cyberattack that cost $15-20M and responded by locking all third-party accounts and migrating wallets. The mechanism was not disclosed; account/key compromise is inferred, and nothing suggests anyone was tricked into signing.

name: CoW Swap
malicious_action: approval/permit-style signatures (and some transactions) granting a drainer contract, rather than the GPv2VaultRelayer, access to victims' tokens
notes: A social-engineering attack on registrar Gandi gave attackers control of cow.fi for about 4.5 hours on Apr 14, 2026. The cloned swap.cow.fi got visitors to 'sign malicious messages or transactions' for a drainer contract (about $1.2M lost per CoW); one Ledger/Rabby victim describes signing a malicious message while approving USDC, and CoW told users to sign approvals only to 0xc92e…0110. The format is the dominant reported one, but the losses were mixed: the largest victim (about half the losses, by their own forum post) typed a seed phrase into a fake prompt, which is KEY_THEFT.

name: Grinex
malicious_action: about $13.7M USDT withdrawn from 54 exchange wallets after access to operational systems
notes: On April 15, 2026 an attacker got into the sanctioned exchange Grinex's operational systems and pulled about $13.7M, mostly TRON USDT, quickly swapping it to TRX and ETH. Grinex blamed Western intelligence agencies and published no technical root cause.

name: Remitano
notes: About $2.7M was drained from Remitano's hot wallet in Sep 2023 after a third-party data breach likely exposed keys or credentials; Tether froze about $1.4M. Custodial key compromise.

name: CoinDCX
malicious_action: liquidity-providing operational account drained via breached internal wallet systems
notes: Bengaluru police say attackers posing as recruiters got a CoinDCX engineer to install malware on his work laptop, then used his access to breach internal wallet systems and drain an operational account (about $44M).

name: Milady Maker
notes: According to founder Charlotte Fang, a rogue Remilia developer diverted about $1M of Bonkler project fees, seized codebases, and took over the MiladyMaker X account to demand more of the treasury. This was insider theft, not an external hack.

name: CF Token
notes: The Creat Future (CF) token on BSC left its _transfer function public. The attacker simply called _transfer to move CF out of the PancakeSwap pair to himself and sold it, about $1.9M.

name: Bithumb
notes: ~3.1M EOS and ~20.2M XRP left Bithumb's hot wallet; Bithumb blamed insiders and found no evidence of an external breach.

name: DeltaPrime
malicious_action: compromised Arbitrum ProxyAdmin key used to upgrade five proxies to malicious implementations
notes: Someone holding the private key of DeltaPrime's Arbitrum ProxyAdmin (a single key, not multisig) upgraded the pool contracts and drained about $6M. The project had employed developers later exposed as DPRK IT workers, but how the key leaked was never confirmed.

name: Kokomo Finance
notes: Kokomo Finance on Optimism carried out an exit scam that took about $4M of user funds. ZachXBT later linked the same operators to the Magnate and Solfire rugs.

name: FixedFloat
notes: FixedFloat lost about $2.8M in a second theft around Apr 1, 2024, which it blamed on the same thieves exploiting a vulnerability in a third-party service. Exchange-side compromise; no user signing.

name: Zoth ZeUSD
malicious_action: compromised deployer upgraded the USD0PPSubVault proxy to a malicious implementation and drained it
notes: The attacker controlled Zoth's deployer key. After a failed attempt the day before, they upgraded the USD0PPSubVault proxy to a contract they had deployed six days earlier and drained about $8.4M. A multinational sanctions-monitoring (MSMT) report attributes it to DPRK.

name: Loopring
notes: The attacker defeated the 2FA of Loopring's Official Guardian recovery service and used social recovery to take ownership of wallets that relied only on that guardian, then moved about $5M out. Recovery-service compromise; victims signed nothing.

name: Terra (LUNA)
notes: From April 12 to 21, 2022, Google search ads sent Terra users to phishing copies of Terra wallet sites that asked for their mnemonic. About 52 wallets were swept to terra1fz57nt6t3nnxel6q77wsmxxdesn7rgy0h27x30 (~$4.31M); this was seed theft, not a deceptive signature.

name: Lympo
malicious_action: 165.2M LMT moved out of operational hot wallets
notes: Hackers got into Lympo's operational hot wallets on Jan 10, 2022, moved 165.2M LMT (about $18.7M) to one address, and swapped it for ETH. How they got access was not disclosed.

name: Arbix Finance
notes: Arbix Finance drained ~$10M of user deposits from its own BSC vaults into 0x4714a26e4e2e1334c80575332ec9eb043b61a2c4, dumped pre-minted ARBX, and deleted its website and social accounts.

name: Monkey Kingdom
malicious_action: SOL transfer draining the wallet to the attacker, presented as a Baepes presale mint
notes: A breach of Grape (a Solana Discord verification tool) let an attacker take over a Monkey Kingdom Discord admin and post a fake Baepes presale link. Users who connected and approved the 'mint' were drained of SOL (~7,000 SOL total; one user lost 650 SOL). No source gives a victim transaction signature.

name: Cork V1
notes: Cork let anyone create a market with an arbitrary redemption asset, and CorkHook's beforeSwap had no caller check. The attacker made a market whose redemption asset was a legitimate market's DS token, called beforeSwap directly with crafted hook data, and redeemed ~$12M of wstETH.

name: Infini
notes: A former contract developer kept 'super admin' rights after handover and used them to drain ~49.5M USDC; Infini sued him (Chen Shanxuan) and three unnamed people in Hong Kong. Reports later linked the funding wallet to the 2026 IoTeX attacker, but no victim signature was involved either way.

name: ALEX
notes: ALEX said the May 2024 exploit used private keys compromised in a phishing attack, which it attributes to Lazarus. With those keys the attacker took control of its XLink bridge on BSC and drained about $4.3M.

name: PEPE
notes: Three former PEPE team members who held multisig keys lowered the multisig threshold and moved about 16 trillion PEPE (~$15M) to exchanges. PEPE's own statement describes it as insider theft.

name: Reaper Farm
notes: Reaper's vault withdraw/redeem path did not check that the caller owned the shares or had an allowance for them, so the attacker redeemed other users' vault shares to himself, about $1.7M on Fantom.

name: KlaySwap
malicious_action: approve to the attacker's fake factory contract 0x3f315f2bfa8452febbc08a9e3a7fdf8872f9527c, then a swap call to it that transferred the tokens to the attacker
notes: A BGP hijack of the IP ranges serving developers.kakao.com, backed by a fraudulently issued TLS certificate, served a malicious kakao.min.js to KLAYswap users for hours on Feb 3, 2022. The script swapped in the attacker's factory and recipient addresses, so deposit and swap flows approved and called 0x3f31…527c, which sent tokens to 0xdfcb…1a0b. 0xccb0… is the 'First Victim Transaction ID' in S2W's post-mortem; 0xaec1… is the same victim's approve in block 82005468, the block S2W cites, which I found via Kaia RPC.

name: AscenDEX
malicious_action: hot wallets drained on Ethereum, BSC and Polygon
notes: AscendEX's hot wallets were compromised on Dec 11, 2021 and about $77M was moved out across three chains. It was an exchange infrastructure breach with no human signing step.
